work_order.understanding:
I reproduced BUG-11 myself before theorising, and it is exactly as reported. From a clean copy of cecee2047ef7a85e371355eeed3eaa50f10d07b3: `node --test` is 489 pass / 0 fail. Inserting one line as the first statement of probeStylesheet — `if (sheet) return { outranking: [], rootReports: [] };` — and changing nothing else leaves it at 489 pass / 0 fail. The probe now reports nothing, ever, and the suite cannot tell.

THE DIAGNOSIS IN THE LAST WORK ORDER WAS NOT WRONG, and I want to be exact about that rather than reaching for a new theory, because 'the plan was wrong' is not the finding and saying it would send the implementer looking for something else. v4 diagnosed BUG-9 and BUG-10 correctly and this run's report says so itself: QA re-ran all 62 cases and every one behaves as v4 stated, with the browser controls measured rather than assumed. Both of those bugs are genuinely fixed. BUG-11 is not a failed diagnosis. It is a fix that was right about its target and wrong about the one artifact in the change whose entire job was to be unfalsifiable.

WHAT v4 GOT WRONG, precisely: it named this exact failure and then built the thing that cannot produce it. risks[3] of the order that produced this PR reads 'The risk is the opposite mistake: deleting the probe because the guard now agrees with it, which is what AC-21's red half is there to catch.' The mitigation built for that sentence was the two real-override rows — an enumeration: put two rows in the table whose expected value only a working probe can produce. But the rows were compared through verdicts(), which returns the UNION of the guard's offenders and the probe's. A union is satisfied whenever EITHER side matches, and every row's expected value is what outrankingPageTitleDeclarations returns on its own, so the probe contributed to nothing in any of the sixteen rows. The rows were present, the risk was named in prose, and the table still could not fail. This is the third time on this issue that a property was stated and then enforced by putting something in a list rather than by making the thing itself unable to pass: v3 enumerated the sites that answer the cascade question, v4 enumerated the literals and then enumerated the rows, and every enumeration was complete while the property went unenforced each time.

THE ASYMMETRY IS THE POINT. A union catches a probe that OVER-reports and is blind to one that UNDER-reports, because a spurious extra finding is absorbed into the guard's correct verdict exactly as silently as a missing one. Under-reporting is the only direction that matters here: the probe's claim is exhaustive over src/web/styles.css, and an exhaustive claim that has stopped being made returns the same [] as an exhaustive claim that has been satisfied. The other two assertions on the probe — `probe.outranking` and `probe.rootReports` deepEqual [] on the clean shipped sheet — are vacuous under the same mutation, since an always-empty probe satisfies them, so nothing anywhere in the file distinguishes 'the probe examined every rule of the shipped sheet' from 'the probe was deleted'.

THIS IS NOT THE 'CRITERION IS WRONG' CASE, and AC-21 is the proof rather than my judgement of it. AC-21 already says, in its own text, 'Both halves are required: the green half on its own is satisfied by deleting the probe'. The criterion predicted this bug down to naming the wrong fix. The code failed to meet a criterion that was right, so AC-21 carries forward byte-for-byte and the code changes. Nothing is renumbered, nothing is dropped, and no criterion is softened: it is precisely AC-21's red half and its how_to_verify that make the difference between this attempt and the last one legible.

BUG-12 IS PRE-EXISTING AND NOT INTRODUCED BY THIS PR, and I am including it deliberately rather than by reflex. It is one 404 on every page load, it is on main unchanged, and everything else in this order is confined to one test file. It goes in because a console error on every load is a standing defect that the next QA run — which is given no memory of this one — will file again, and because it already cost this run a muddled reading: the 25-shell walk can only report '0 console errors' once the page is past first load. The fix is a declared icon and one static route, and I checked it in a real browser rather than assuming it: the implicit /favicon.ico request is present in the baseline network log and absent from the fixed one. If a maintainer would rather this PR stayed test-only, the three favicon files drop out whole without touching the BUG-11 fix; that lever is stated in risks rather than buried.
work_order.root_cause:
The union at test/web/pages.test.js:3469-3476. `verdicts()` returns [...new Set([...outrankingPageTitleDeclarations(...).map(one => one.selector + ' ' + one.group), ...probe.outranking, ...probe.rootReports])], and every row of the BUG-10 table is asserted as that union deepEqual-equals the row's expected. The guard alone returns each row's expected: [] for the fourteen no-op rows, ['#main h1 font-size'] and ['#main h1 line-height'] for the two real overrides. So the predicate is satisfied whenever EITHER input matches, the probe's contribution to every one of the sixteen rows is nil, and the comparison cannot fail when the probe reports nothing — the one direction a check that exists to hold the probe honest has to fail in. It fails only on over-reporting, because a spurious extra finding is absorbed into the same union. The two remaining assertions on the probe, `probe.outranking` and `probe.rootReports` deepEqual [] on the clean shipped sheet, are vacuous under the same mutation since an always-empty probe satisfies them, so no assertion in the file distinguishes a probe that examined every rule of src/web/styles.css from a probe that was deleted.

Underneath it is the shape v4 stated and did not apply to its own new code. v4's root_cause says a decision in this file keeps getting 'pinned to a literal instead of to the thing the decision is about'; this is that sentence one level up. The table's decision is 'the guard and the probe agree about the same rule'. The thing that decision is about is two independent verdicts. It was pinned instead to a single merged verdict, which is a literal for the agreement rather than the agreement itself — and a literal that stops matching is quiet rather than loud, which is what v4's own sentence predicts and what the file then demonstrates. The missing step in all three instances is the same one: the 25-shell count anchor, the four class-literal fixtures, and now the table that was built to anchor the probe were each enforced by adding cases, and in each case nothing required the enforcement mechanism itself to be shown capable of failing. Adding the rows that would catch a neutered probe is not the same as making the probe's silence detectable, and this bug is the difference between the two.
work_order.approach:
One test file for BUG-11, three small files for BUG-12. No production behaviour changes; no cascade rule, fixture, class, message, or pinned anchor is touched.

The difference from v4 is one sentence and it is the whole answer to why an attempt with a correct diagnosis still failed. v4 made the table's ROWS right; the rows were already the right rows. This makes the table's COMPARISON a tested artifact. Not 'add the cases that would catch it' — the cases were there — but 'hand the comparison a broken input and require it to notice'.

1 — ONE COMPARISON, NAMED, AND NEVER A UNION. Hoist the two sides to module scope beside the table as `guardVerdictOf(sheetText)` and `probeVerdictOf(sheetText)`, and replace `verdicts()` with `disagreementsIn({ extra, expected, guard, probe })`, which returns the list of sides that do not match the row — 'the guard disagrees about ...', 'the probe disagrees about ...' — and [] when both do. Each row is then asserted deepEqual [] against that, so a failure names which of the two implementations drifted instead of reporting a merged list that matches whenever one side is right. The guard is now genuinely held to the same expected value the probe is held to, which it never was. All sixteen rows, their order, their expected values and their claims stay exactly as they are; only the comparison changes.

2 — THE ROWS BECOME A NAMED TABLE. Hoist the row array to a module-scope `BUG_10_ROWS` so the test in step 3 reads this table rather than a second copy of it. Two copies is how the last two attempts each wrote the same rule down twice and enforced it once.

3 — THE COMPARISON IS REQUIRED TO FAIL, IN-SUITE. A new test, 'BUG-11: the agreement table is a comparison that can fail', walks BUG_10_ROWS with the real guard verdict and `probe: []` — a probe that reports nothing — and requires the comparison to return exactly two disagreements, the two real-override rows, and nothing else. That one assertion closes three doors at once, and I verified each by mutation on a copy of the tree at cecee2047, not by reasoning: neutering probeStylesheet turns the BUG-10 table red (489 pass / 1 fail); collapsing disagreementsIn back into the union turns this new test red (489 pass / 1 fail); deleting the two real-override rows turns this new test red (489 pass / 1 fail). So the thirteen green rows are green because both sides are silent rather than because one side is silent, and the wrong fix AC-21 forbids — buying the green half by deleting the probe — is no longer available at any of the three doors. This is deliberately the mechanism v4 did not use: v4 answered 'how do we know the probe is honest' with a table asserting an aggregate, and this answers it by breaking an input and watching the predicate. The file's existing idiom is the same instinct at a smaller target — the pinning test at :1609 reads the file's own source to catch a deleted call site — and this applies it to a predicate rather than a string, which is strictly stronger because a neutered predicate becomes a failing assertion rather than an absence nobody notices.

4 — BUG-12: declare the icon and serve it. `<link rel="icon" href="/assets/favicon.svg" type="image/svg+xml">` in the head beside the stylesheet link, a GET /assets/favicon.svg route in src/api/routes.js beside the other two asset routes, and a 16x16 SVG at src/web/favicon.svg. Verified against a running preview: the implicit /favicon.ico request is in the network log before the change and gone after it.

5 — KEEP WHAT IS ALREADY RIGHT. All sixteen rows, both value predicates, the class-literal audit, the in-memory coordinated-rename case, the revert asymmetry, the pinning tests at :1609 and the 25-shell anchor. The 489 cases on the clean tree are the regression suite for v4's work and not one of them moves; the new test makes it 490, and I ran the full suite with both fixes in place to confirm nothing else shifts.

Holding the guard to the row's expected value is a new obligation that did not exist before: the table used to be satisfied by the guard alone, so a row could in principle have an expected value only the probe produces. Every one of the sixteen has been checked against the guard, and all sixteen agree, but a future row added to this table must satisfy BOTH sides or the table will be red. residual_risks: The fix makes the probe's SILENCE detectable and does not make a MISREAD detectable. A probe that still reads every rule of src/web/styles.css and gets one of them wrong returns a non-empty, plausible verdict, and neither the guard nor the falsifiability test can tell that from a correct one. QA names this as the coverage gap it could not reach, and it is the same gap after this change. What would close it is a differential over a much broader set of sheets than sixteen rows, and an open-ended mutation matrix is how this issue reached eight plan attempts; broadening the table deliberately, one family of cases at a time, is a separate piece of work and not a thing to bolt on here.

The guard-versus-probe agreement is a claim about the shipped stylesheet and the sixteen appended rules. Both implementations share `cls`, the resolved element chain, the reader and the tokenizer, so a defect in any of those four is invisible to the comparison by construction — the two answers would be wrong the same way. This is unchanged from v4 and is inherent to comparing two implementations that share their front end; the class-literal audit and the pinning tests are what cover the shared parts.

The BUG-11 test asserts the comparison against a stub probe that returns nothing. A future change that made the probe report through a different shape — say one array instead of two — would need that stub updated, and if it were updated carelessly to mirror the new shape the test could go vacuous again. The assertion's value is in the EXPECTED side (exactly the two real-override rows), which is data the test does not derive from the probe, so a careless stub update is visible as a changed expectation rather than as silence.
